news.title: U.S. Secretary of Education Linda McMahon Visits Missouri on Returning Education to the States Tour
news.content:
September 16, 2026
ST. LOUIS, MO –
Today, U.S. Secretary of Education Linda McMahon visited Missouri on her
Returning Education to the States Tour
.
Secretary McMahon began her visit at Gideon #37, a small, rural elementary school in southeast Missouri. There, she toured the campus facilities and participated in a rural workforce roundtable with local business leaders to discuss strengthening community-driven economic opportunities. She then traveled to the Cape Girardeau Career & Technology Center (Cape CTC) for a lunch prepared and served by culinary arts students, followed by a tour of the school's hands-on instructional labs for its electrical, welding, automotive, and construction programs.
The tour concluded at Washington University in St. Louis (WashU), where Secretary McMahon met with the leadership of the Gephardt Institute for Civic and Community Engagement, participated in a Rural Health Roundtable focused on regional medical access, and sat down with Chancellor Andrew D. Martin to discuss the intersection of higher education and community development.
“Missouri is the 42nd state visited on my Returning Education to the States Tour, and what I saw here perfectly illustrates why local communities must drive educational decision-making,”
said U.S. Secretary of Education Linda McMahon.
“From the workforce roundtable at Gideon and the hands-on career training labs at Cape CTC to our regional development discussions at Washington University, Missouri educators are successfully designing localized pipelines that meet specific community needs. These collaborative local efforts reinforce our broader commitment to providing states with the flexibility and resources necessary to best serve their own students.”
Background:
On her Returning Education to the States Tour, Secretary McMahon is traveling to all 50 states to hear directly from teachers, parents, and community leaders about what is working in their communities for their students and compile a toolkit of best practices to distribute to states.
Learn more about Secretary McMahon’s Returning Education to the States Tour
here
.

news.title: U.S. Department of Education and U.S. Department of State Open Foreign Funding Investigations into Duke University and the University of North Dakota
news.content:
September 16, 2026
Yesterday, the U.S. Department of Education (ED) and the U.S. Department of State (State) opened foreign funding investigations into Duke University (Duke) and the University of North Dakota (UND) after reviews of university records indicated the submission of incomplete, inaccurate, and untimely disclosures.
Both Duke and UND are research institutions that have received significant taxpayer support for the development of critical and emerging technologies. Pursuant to Section 117 of the Higher Education Act of 1965, postsecondary institutions receiving federal financial assistance must disclose foreign source gifts and contracts with a value of $250,000 or more annually.
These investigations follow yesterday’s House Foreign Affairs Subcommittee hearing that examined the ‘covert malign influence’ operations involving China and Cuba.
“Unfortunately, it appears that both Duke and UND have provided untimely and incomplete foreign funding disclosures, which include erroneously identifying certain governmental partners as ‘non-governmental,’”
said Under Secretary of Education Nicholas Kent.
“Section 117 requires that institutions of higher education clearly and accurately report their foreign financial ties in a timely manner — to ensure public transparency and as a condition of participating in the federal student aid programs. We expect these universities will cooperate fully. The Department of Education and the Department of State will continue to work together to vigorously ensure the integrity and accountability of our nation’s colleges and universities in reporting their foreign gifts and contracts.”
"Our reviews found real gaps in how Duke and UND have handled their Section 117 obligations — disclosures submitted late, key details left out, and at least one foreign government partner mischaracterized as a non-governmental entity,"
said Under Secretary of State for Public Diplomacy Sarah B. Rogers.
"The law is clear: colleges and universities must report foreign gifts and contracts accurately and on time.  We expect Duke and UND will work with us transparently as this review moves forward. The State Department remains committed to partnering with the Department of Education to hold higher education institutions accountable for full and honest disclosure of their foreign funding."
Investigation into Duke University’s Foreign Financial Disclosures
In 2013, Duke partnered with China’s Wuhan University (WU) to establish the Duke Kunshan University (DKU) in Kunshan, Jiangsu in (China). WU is overseen by China’s State Administration of Science, Technology and Industry for National Defense (SASTIND), which plays a key role in China’s national defense science and technology innovation system, and “
trains [China’s] cyber warfare specialists
.”
As described in the
NOI
, the Chinese government requires joint venture universities, like DKU, to be governed by China’s Ministry of Education and include a “party-run [CCP] unit [to] monitor operations and have a say over big administrative tasks.” Cooperation by the DKU joint institute is mandatory. An examination of DKU’s leadership and governance indicates that it is comprised of prominent Chinese government and Wuhan University officials.
In August 2026, the U.S. Department of War issued a formal notification to Duke University, among other research universities, directing it to initiate immediate and comprehensive reviews of its academic, financial, and research collaborations with foreign entities of concerns.
To verify Duke University’s compliance with the law and the accuracy of its previous disclosures, the agencies’ investigation requires that Duke produce certain records within thirty (30) calendar days, including, but not limited to:
Various tax records related to Duke’s extensive foreign involvements as provided to the Internal Revenue Service (IRS), U.S. Department of the Treasury (Treasury), and Federal Elections Commission (FEC);
Verification of the adequacy of institutional controls, documents, and records related to Duke’s Section 117 compliance structure;
Records related to Duke’s agreements with foreign entities regarding international students, faculty, and research personnel;
Records related to Duke’s extensive international research collaborations;
Records related to the participation of Duke personnel in foreign government talent programs; and
Copies of Duke’s reportable foreign gifts, grants, and contracts.
Investigation into the University of North Dakota’s Foreign Financial Disclosures
UND is a recipient of significant federal awards in support of its School of Aerospace’s “uncrewed air systems” efforts. Those efforts, critical to U.S. national security interests, have also drawn significant investment and involvement to UND by Chinese aviation companies known to have close associations with China’s military.

news.title: U.S. Department of Education Honors Constitution Day, Calls on Schools to Strengthen Civic Literacy and Invite Routine Recitation of the Pledge of Allegiance
news.content:
September 16, 2026
In observance of Constitution Day on September 17th and following America’s historic 250th anniversary of independence, U.S. Secretary of Education Linda McMahon today issued a Dear Colleague Letter to all education leaders and teachers, urging them to strengthen civic learning and provide routine opportunities for students to recite the Pledge of Allegiance.
The call to action addresses an urgent need to close a widening gap in civic literacy and declining national pride among young Americans. Pointing to recent troubling data, Secretary McMahon noted that fewer than six in 10 Americans aged 18 to 29 feel “very proud” to be American. Furthermore, national assessments reveal a profound civic literacy crisis, with only 22 percent of eighth graders reaching proficiency in civics and just 13 percent doing so in U.S. history—leaving the next generation largely unprepared to actively participate in civic life.
“To thrive for the next 250 years, we must understand, cherish, and claim the ideals, history, responsibilities, and civic traditions that unite us,”
wrote U.S. Secretary of Education Linda McMahon.
“With 31 simple words, for a minute a day, students connect themselves to this great American story, take ownership of their citizenship, feel pride in their country, and become architects of the nation’s future.”
Over the past year, the U.S. Department of Education has worked to revitalize civic engagement through several national initiatives, including:
The
History Rocks!
Tour:
Visiting schools across all 50 states to bring history to life in honor of our nation’s 250th birthday for students with interactive games and competitions;
The Presidential 1776 Award for Civics:
Challenging thousands of high school students from across the country to demonstrate advanced knowledge of American governance and history; and
Targeted Grant Competitions:
Funding educational programs dedicated to teaching American history, citizenship, government, and geography.
Secretary McMahon noted that while this guidance introduces no new federal mandates, it serves as a gentle reminder of the power of civic tradition. State and local leaders are encouraged to invite voluntary, daily opportunities for the Pledge of Allegiance in harmony with local policies. In doing so, school practices should always respect students’ constitutional rights, including protections affirmed by the U.S. Supreme Court regarding voluntary participation.

news.title: U.S. Secretary of Education Linda McMahon Joins Cleveland Browns for “Stay in the Game!” Attendance Celebration
news.content:
September 15, 2026
Cleveland, OH –
Today, U.S. Secretary of Education Linda McMahon visited Cleveland, Ohio for a celebration event with the NFL team, the Cleveland Browns, on their premier youth outreach initiative, the
Stay in the Game!
program.
Honoring local students from the Intergenerational Schools, the celebration recognized 40 K-8 students who were uniquely selected by their teachers for exemplary school attendance records. Secretary McMahon welcomed students at the facility for a special program featuring academic motivation remarks, an interactive tour, and outdoor field day games.
“Showing up to learn every single day is the most fundamental step a student can take toward achieving long-term success,”
said U.S. Secretary of Education Linda McMahon.
“To set our youth up for tomorrow's economic realities, we must look beyond standard models — which is why this unique partnership brilliantly uses the universal appeal of sports to connect with children exactly where they are. It was a true privilege to witness this in action while celebrating 40 young Ohioans whose commitment to everyday school attendance sets a powerful example.”
Background:
Launched in 2019, the
Stay in the Game! Attendance Network
combats chronic absenteeism by connecting schools with proven resources and expert support. Originally founded by the Cleveland Browns Foundation, the Ohio Department of Education and Workforce, and Harvard’s Proving Ground, the network is now managed by Battelle.
Stay in the Game!
plays a key role in connecting districts and education leaders to the resources and tools that can meaningfully improve attendance, including:
Attendance campaign materials to use in schools and community
Incentives and activities aimed at students to reward good and improved attendance
Peer learning opportunities to meaningfully impact attendance

news.title: U.S. Department of Education Approves Workforce Pell Grant Programs in Nebraska
news.content:
September 14, 2026
Today, the U.S. Department of Education (the Department) approved three Workforce Pell Grant programs in Nebraska, marking it the third state in the nation to receive program approvals. Eligible students at Metropolitan Community College can now use Federal Pell Grant dollars to enroll in its Phlebotomy Technician, Pharmacy Technician, and CompTia Tech+ with Google IT Support programs. These programs aim to prepare students for key healthcare and information technology professions.
The new Workforce Pell program enables eligible students to apply and access grant funds for short-term, accredited, workforce-aligned programs that can be completed in as little as 8 weeks. Established under President Trump’s signature Working Families Tax Cuts Act and launched by the Department earlier this summer, this reform broadens access to postsecondary education beyond traditional four-year career pathways by supporting high-quality, affordable credentials that can be earned quickly and with less student debt.
“Workforce Pell is all about putting American students and businesses first, propelling students into high-wage, in-demand careers throughout the Cornhusker State,”
said Under Secretary of Education Nicholas Kent
. “Nebraska’s new approved programs underscore the Trump Administration’s commitment to creating more affordable, faster routes to enter the workforce.”
"This is tremendous news and it represents tremendous opportunity for getting people the technical training they need to take advantage of high-demand, high-paying, and highly rewarding careers right here in Nebraska,”
said Nebraska Governor Jim Pillen.
“The funding that will allow students to participate in these short-term programs represents an investment, one that will pay off in dividends. I'm appreciative of the state-federal collaboration that has made this happen so quickly."
“Students shouldn’t have to choose between getting the skills they need and spending years in school or taking on significant debt,”
said Metropolitan Community College President Randy Schmailzl
. “Workforce Pell opens the door to faster, more affordable pathways into good careers, and Metropolitan Community College was ready to walk through that door. We’ve built our short-term workforce programs around what students and employers need, and now eligible students have another way to access those opportunities through Workforce Pell and the short-term education model we’ve been building for our community.”
To qualify for Workforce Pell, a program must meet rigorous earnings, job placement, and completion benchmarks; have been in operation for at least one year; and receive approval from both the Governor and the U.S. Secretary of Education. These three programs meet these standards, opening the door for students who are seeking to enter the healthcare and information technology professions without taking on extreme student debt burdens.
Background
Last year, President Trump signed the Working Families Tax Cuts Act into law, which established criteria for short-term programs to gain eligibility to receive Workforce Pell.
The Department conducted
negotiated rulemaking
to establish the regulatory framework for Workforce Pell. The
final rule
implementing Workforce Pell was published on May 18, 2026, and became effective on July 1, 2026.
On August 4, 2026, the Department
approved
the nation’s first Workforce Pell grant program at Iowa Central Community College to prepare Emergency Medical Technicians. On August 19, 2026, the Department
approved
the nation’s second Workforce Pell grant program at Ivy Tech Community College to train Clinical Medical Assistants.
In coordination with state workforce boards, Governors across the country are currently identifying education and training programs that meet the high-skill, high-wage, or in-demand criteria for Workforce Pell eligibility. This process enables state leaders to designate programs that are well positioned to improve employment outcomes and generate strong economic returns for workers and their states.
